This week, I've been quietly working on something very close to my heart.

Today, I can finally share it.

I'm honoured to be featured in Sydney Weekend in this Saturday's @dailytelegraph (alongside an extraordinary group of women, in a deeply thoughtful piece by @lisamayoh on burnout: how it sneaks up on us, breaks us down, and what it actually takes to rebuild.

Two years ago, I hit a wall I couldn't push through. Anxiety, exhaustion, a nervous system that had been running in fight-or-flight for decades. Recovery wasn't a reset: it was a re-learning.

Out of that period came The Sacred 60: 60 rituals, practices and tools that helped me survive burnout and slowly come back to myself: shaped by lived experience, doctors, scientists, therapists, and conversations from the Beautiful Inside by @beauticate podcast.

For now, it's exclusive to Telegraph readers.
If you pick up the Saturday paper, you'll find the interview, and access to the guide inside.

A heartfelt thank you to @timhunter for capturing this chapter so beautifully, @jess_diez for my makeup, and to Lisa for the care, depth and humanity in her storytelling. It's also a follow-up to the beautiful feature Lisa wrote on my journey back in 2024, when I first launched the Beautiful Inside podcast: a moment that marked the beginning of a very different chapter for me. I'll link that article in stories, too, because together they tell the fuller picture.

We'll be sharing The Sacred 60 with the @beauticate community very soon. But today, this one belongs to the paper.

More tomorrow.

CW: Chronic illness, pain, medical gaslighting, perimenopause

Around 40, when my health took a nose dive, perimenopause wasn't a thing yet so I began all the investigations, saw specialists and tried different therapies. At its worst, I ended up in hospital, unable to eat, unable to function.

Mum said it's my gallbladder (she went through similar) but nothing shows up in scans or scopes. A pain specialist said it's degenerative arthritis - consistent with age related wear and tear. But I'm 44... not 88!
Some say "it's stress - you work too much." Others say, "Oh, it's just perimenopause."

And maybe it is... Or maybe perimenopause was the hormonal wildfire that lit the fuse. But here's what they don't tell you:

- That "perimenopause" is often code for we don't actually know what's going on.
- That women are frequently gaslit when their bloods look normal but their bodies feel broken.
- That chronic illness doesn't always have one neat label: it's a puzzle.
- That you need to become your own advocate, your own researcher, your own hope-holder.
- That the search for answers can feel lonely, overwhelming... and also deeply empowering.

If you're in it too: lost in your symptoms, dismissed by doctors, wondering if you'll ever feel okay again, I see you.
You're not crazy. You're not alone.
You're just in the part no one talks about.

If this story resonates, I'd love to hear yours.
Drop a heart if you've ever felt dismissed, misdiagnosed, or just plain fed up.
You're not alone.
My morning longevity ritual: a small yet mighty breakfast to fuel my day.

These 5 biohacks have changed my energy, mood, and mornings:

1. Tongue scraping
This might sound a little odd, but once you try it, you'll never go back. I scrape my tongue the second I wake up — it removes overnight bacteria buildup, boosts oral health, and (apparently) kickstarts digestion by stimulating organs via the tongue. It's Ayurvedic, it's satisfying, and honestly, your toothbrush could never.

2. Mouth taping
I know, I know. It sounds unhinged. But mouth taping has been the single biggest game-changer for my sleep. I use a tiny strip of surgical tape across my lips at night — it gently trains me to breathe through my nose, which helps with oxygen intake, nervous system regulation and even snoring. I wake up feeling properly rested, not like I've been in a bar fight with my pillow.

3. Legs up the wall
If I've had a stressful day or I've been on my feet, I'll lie on the floor, shimmy my legs up a wall, and just be. It improves circulation, calms the nervous system, and helps drain lymphatic fluid — and it's wildly calming. No special gear, no excuses. Just legs + wall = bliss.

4. Mushroom coffee
I swapped my boring old latte for this earthy little ritual — a blend of Lion's Mane, Cordyceps and sometimes even Shiitake from @lifecykel. I mix the extracts into my almond-milk coffee and love the rich, grounding flavour. It's become a mindful moment in my morning — a calm, steady start to the day without the caffeine jitters.

5. Breathwork while driving
This one is sneaky but so powerful. Whenever I get in the car, I automatically do a few rounds of box breathing or 4-6-7 breathing — inhale for 4, hold for 6, exhale for 7. It's become a little anchor in my day. My shoulders drop, my glutes unclench (lol but true), and I suddenly become aware of the trees, the light, the air around me. Just a tiny moment of mindfulness... in traffic. Road rage - be gone! Would you try any of these?
Or are you already doing some of them too?

Busy Mum/Peri-brain/ADHD Hack #1: Environmental Design + Habit Stacking
Between motherhood, midlife hormones, and running a business, remembering to do the thing is half the battle. That's where this trick comes in...

I keep my LED mask on the coffee table, right next to my neck roller. Why? Because if it's out of sight, it's out of mind. But when it's right there in my space — and next to something I already use — I actually remember to do it.

This is called environmental design, and it's a game-changer for ADHD, neurodivergent, and perimenopausal brains — all of which struggle with working memory and follow-through.

Habit stacking (from @jamesclearatomichabits) is about linking a new habit to something you already do, like:
- Putting your supplements next to your toothbrush
- Keeping a gratitude journal on your pillow
- Placing your gym gear next to the kettle if you always start the day with tea

Environmental Design is used in behavioural psychology to support memory and habit formation. For ADHD and perimenopausal brains (both of which are prone to forgetfulness, fog, and overwhelm), visual cues in the environment significantly increase follow-through.
According to Atomic Habits by James Clear, "You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems." In other words, if you want habits to stick, your space has to support them.
Studies show that ADHD brains benefit from visible, physical reminders — especially when those cues are in high-traffic areas of the home. The more frictionless the habit, the higher the compliance.
In perimenopause, 40-68% of women report cognitive symptoms like forgetfulness, brain fog and mental fatigue — especially when juggling family and career. Environmental design becomes a powerful ally here too.
If your brain needs a nudge, make it visual. Make it obvious.
And make your environment work for you.
Would you try this?

Wellness propaganda I fell for... and I'm better for it.
I used to think self-care meant bath bombs and green juice. Now I know it looks more like:

- Red light therapy — It's been clinically shown to support mitochondrial health, reduce inflammation and boost collagen. I do mine while meditating or journaling — double win.
- Barefoot walks — I know it sounds a bit woo-woo, but grounding works. Walking barefoot on sand or grass helps regulate the nervous system and reduce cortisol. Nature's anti-anxiety tool.
- Reishi before bed (@lifecykel) — My nervous system's nightcap alternative. Reishi is often celebrated in wellness circles for its calming and adaptogenic reputation — I find it helps me unwind without wine.
- Chaga in my water (@lifecykel) — My morning ritual. Chaga is rich in natural antioxidants and minerals — I love the earthy flavour and ritual of starting my day this way.
- HRT and herbs — A game-changer for perimenopause. I'm combining low-dose HRT with herbal support for balance, sleep and emotional steadiness.
- Daily magnesium — My non-negotiable for feeling relaxed and easing muscle tension.
- Creatine in my coffee — Not just for gym bros. Creatine has become my brain and body support as I've gotten older.
- Being strong, not skinny — This mental shift alone has changed how I feel in my body. Strength is the goal. The rest follows.
- Sleep > hustle — I used to worship productivity. Now I try and prioritise rest and if that means skipping my workout or letting those late night work sessions go then so be it. True repair happens when we stop.
- Energy healing and inner child work — Therapy helped me meet the younger me who thought she had to be perfect to be loved. Now I try to check in with her daily. She tells me what I really need to nourish myself.

These aren't trends. They're tools. They helped me crawl back from burnout and build a version of wellness that feels grounded, joyful and sustainable.

"I started to believe the things strangers were saying about me."

@susanyara opens up about the backlash she faced and what happens when the noise becomes so loud, it starts to shape how you see yourself.

When there are gaps in the story, people fill them. And those assumptions can quickly spiral into something much bigger than the truth.

What began as a business decision during an uncertain time became a turning point. Without full transparency around how she became a co-founder of @naturium, the narrative shifted and she found herself at the centre of it.

And when you hear something enough times, even if it isn't true, it can start to feel real.

If you don't already know her, Susan is one of the original beauty YouTubers who built a global audience through honesty, and went on to co-found @naturium, a brand she later sold in a deal reportedly worth $514 million.

But her story goes far beyond business. It's about navigating criticism, rebuilding trust, and learning how to hold your own in a very loud world.

In the latest episode of Beautiful Inside by Beauticate, we talk about all of it.

I used to think LED was just a "nice to have" for skin.

Now it's one of the few things I rely on for both beauty and wellness.

Yes, it helps with collagen, inflammation and overall skin quality. But what surprised me most is how much I reach for it when I'm not feeling great.

When I'm run down, sick, or dealing with pain, this is one of the first things I layer on. It's low effort, calming, and feels like I'm actively supporting my body, not just waiting it out.

Over time, it's become less about anti-ageing and more about maintenance. Skin, energy, recovery. The things that actually matter day to day.

This little setup might look like a lot. But it's really just one of a few wellness protocols I genuinely swear by.

The kind that earn their place because they work.

Community is becoming one of the most powerful forms of wellness.
In this episode of Beautiful Inside, @sigourneycantelo shares the story behind @beauticate's monthly Walk & Talk gatherings on Sydney's Northern Beaches - a simple idea that has created a meaningful connection for so many women.
Each month, we gather at a different beach to walk, talk and spend time together without an agenda, expectation or pressure. Just conversation, fresh air and connection. And breathwork with the amazing Brooke @luxewellnesscollective
What Sig has loved most is hearing the stories unfold. Women sharing experiences. Offering support. Finding common ground. Creating friendships.
And beyond the emotional benefits, there are physical ones too. Walking can help lower cortisol levels, while rhythmic movement supports nervous system regulation, making it one of the simplest and most accessible wellbeing practices available.
In a culture that often tells us to do more, this is a reminder that sometimes what we really need is to slow down and connect.

Sometimes the smallest wellness upgrades make the biggest difference.
In this episode of Beautiful Inside, Sigourney Cantelo shares one of the products that's become an unexpected staple in her daily routine: a heated neck massager that helps ease tension, stress and tight muscles after long days at her desk.
What she loves most is how simple it is. The heated massage nodules work through the neck and shoulders, creating a sense of relief that's both immediate and deeply relaxing.
And there's good reason it feels so effective. Heat therapy increases blood flow to tense muscles, while massage helps reduce pain signals, release knots and encourage muscle relaxation throughout the body.
For anyone carrying stress in their shoulders, dealing with desk-related tension or simply craving a little more comfort in their day, this might be one of those surprisingly helpful discoveries.

Beautiful People, I'm beyond excited (and quietly freaking out) to share something deeply personal and incredibly close to my heart with you today. Beautiful Inside by Beauticate launches today, marking a new chapter for us at Beauticate. This isn't just another podcast — it's a journey into what truly makes us beautiful, inside and out.

Last year, life threw me some unexpected challenges that left me feeling like I couldn't keep up. After years of pushing through, I made the terrifying decision to check myself into a treatment centre to deal with anxiety and some hard stuff I went through as a kid. It wasn't easy, but it was transformative. This experience became the driving force behind Beautiful Inside, where I aim to destigmatise mental health discussions and empower all of us to embrace our vulnerabilities with grace.

In this podcast, I'll be sharing candid stories — my own and those of incredible guests like Trinny Woodall, Pip Edwards, and Poppy King — who have faced their own battles and emerged stronger. Together, we'll cover their mental health journeys, self-care and daily routines the profound link between inner peace and outer radiance. We'll also be talking to experts in aesthetics, longevity, wellness and mindset to uncover their secrets to looking and feeling our best.

But that's not all — what sets Beautiful Inside apart is the way we will bring the stories to life. As a video pod, we'll be filming in the very spaces that define our guests' lives, from their pantries to walk-in wardrobes, surrounded by all their personal stories and treasures. A regular spot will be The Sacred Six: the products and practices our guests swear by for inner and outer wellbeing.

This podcast marks a new era for Beauticate, where we continue to celebrate resilience, authenticity, and the courage to live boldly. Thank you all for being part of this incredible community. I hope Beautiful Inside will inspire, empower, and uplift you, just as it has me.

Mum was wrong about that one. I've been shaving my place (fancy term: dermaplaning) on and off for the last year and I promise, I don't have a big black beard sprouting when I skip a week. It grows back soft and fluffy like the peachy fuzz that it always was. I like doing it because it gives the most beautiful smooth babies bottom effect. Skincare absorbs better and makeup sits beautifully. It's like a deep exfoliation. I just have to find the time to do it. But when I do I'm never disappointed. The trick is to use a facial oil and blade in direction of the hair growth - not against as you do when you shave your legs. Dermaplane tools are a bit easier to manoeuvre and result in less nicks than razors, but in a pinch you could use a razor. I have from time to time but it did make me nervous. This one is by @bondiblades and I liked it. I used the beautiful @mvskintherapy facial booster oil. Smells like heaven and so soothing.

The other day when @drsteve_crimston @allsaintclinic was prepping me for re-entry into the world after a very intense session of laser, he popped a sunscreen on my skin and mentioned that it's essential when you've got pigmentation to use a TINTED sunscreen! I have rarely heard that clever little factoid before, and surprisingly he that it's not just to hide your pigment. He explained that the extra layers of pigment protect your skin even further! @mesoestetic.australia Meso Protect is one example of a tinted SPF 50. there are plenty of tinted sunscreens on the market. Always read the label and follow the directions for use. Sunscreen should always be used in addition to hats, protective clothing and common sense (reapplying every two hours).
Feeling good comes from within or from underneath, and while not every day or moment is good for me, I'm feeling good today! What makes you feel good?

"In greeting each morning remind yourself of Dadirri by blessing yourself with the following; 'Let tiny drops of stillness fall gently through my day.' I'm so enjoying reading @juliabaird's incredible book 'Phosphorescence: on awe, wonder, and the things that sustain you when the world goes dark'. Trying to steal away for little moments of stillness, whenever I can. It's a powerful reminder that little miracles do exist - every day.

A common beauty misstep we encounter is people applying more foundation than they truly need. Instead of slicking on a uniform layer of product across the face without a thought, assess your face everyday to figure out where your skin actually needs coverage. While you might want to cover your jawline acne with foundation followed by concealer, you could go lighter on your cheeks and forehead if you're comfortable with leaving your natural complexion there au naturel.
